He saw Dab-Dab diving in and out of a pond.
And sitting on a large tree branch, Polynesia was chatting to another colorful bird.
Suddenly Tommy let out a scream.
A large black snake was sliding over his foot. He jumped.
"Well, I told him to move his foot, didn't I?" hissed the reptile.
"That's Stanley. Don't worry, he's harmless," Dr. Dolittle said, smiling.
"Do you have any lions or tigers?" asked Tommy.
"I'd like to, but they would eat up all the other animals," the doctor said sadly.
"Oh, you have a deer!" Tommy pointed excitedly.
"No, that's not a deer," the doctor said.
Tommy could not believe his eyes!
The creature had two heads.
"Look at him staring," said one head.
"How rude!" remarked the other head.
"It's his first time seeing you, that's all," the doctor said kindly.
"Come here, Tommy," the doctor called out.
"This is the rarest animal in the world.
It's the pushmi-pullyu, from Africa."
Tommy walked over to it nervously.
"Can I get back to my breakfast, Doctor?" said the pushmi head.
"I'm so hungry."
Tommy gently touched the creature.
"Well, at least he doesn't scratch," said the pullyu head.
Tommy was amazed.
"It's a wonderful garden, Doctor," he said.
"But it's a lot of work." The doctor sighed.
"I could use some help to look after all the animals."
Tommy's heart leaped.
"I could help you, Dr. Dolittle," he said excitedly.
"Yes, I do need an assistant," the doctor replied thoughtfully.
"I'm a hard worker and I do love animals," Tommy said eagerly.
The doctor rubbed his chin.
"I think it's a great idea," Polynesia said.
Tommy looked at the doctor hopefully.
"All right, Tommy.
If your parents agree, you can be my assistant," smiled the doctor.
Tommy let out such a loud shout of joy that all the animals stopped and stared.
"Humans are so strange," remarked the pushmi-pullyu to itself.
"And they say we're loud!" quacked Dab-Dab.
That afternoon, Dr. Dolittle returned home with Tommy.
The doctor told Tommy's parents about Tommy's idea.
Tommy listened anxiously as they talked.
"I will teach Tommy everything I know," Dr. Dolittle promised.
"He will learn to read and write, and a great deal more."
Tommy saw his parents smile at each other.
His heart leapt with excitement.
"Tommy will make a fine assistant, I am certain," said the doctor.
So his parents let Tommy go.
As he left his home, strolling beside the great doctor, Tommy was bursting with pride.
It wasn't easy being an assistant, though.
"This is the chicken feed," Polynesia explained.
"But be careful that the raccoons don't steal the food."
"Rufus! You stay away!" squawked one chicken.
"I'm just passing by," the raccoon said innocently.
Every day Tommy learned something new.
"Did you irritate Coco again, Franny?" the doctor sternly asked a crying lamb.
"Of course not, Dr. Dolittle!
He just has a bad temper," Franny complained.
"What's going on?" whispered Tommy.
"Franny and Coco don't get along," Polynesia answered.
"Who's Coco?" asked Tommy.
"A chimpanzee with a short tail.
He can't hang from trees like other monkeys," Polynesia explained.
"So Franny teases him and Coco bites her."
The doctor put some medicine on Franny's sore bite.
"Ouch!" baaa-ed the lamb.
Being an assistant meant helping the doctor with many things.
This included learning the language of the wiff-waff.
The doctor pulled his head out of the fish tank and cooed:
"Boodi-bob-hop-sop."
Tommy stared at him blankly.
"Boodi-bob . . . oh, sorry, Tommy." Dr. Dolittle chuckled.
"I was speaking to you in pigeon language."
Tommy smiled.
"Can you get me some more water?"
Dr. Dolittle asked, this time in English.
Every chance she got, Polynesia helped Tommy learn the animals' language.
Tommy and Polynesia spent hours in the garden.
Tommy was anxious to learn, but it wasn't easy.
Tommy listened and watched a horse carefully.
"Now what is the horse saying?" Polynesia whispered.
"I am getting so fat!" the horse neighed.
"You're not! Don't be silly," mooed a nearby cow.
Tommy turned to Polynesia and tried to interpret.
"The horse is angry at the cow," he said, "because she eats too much."
Polynesia covered her mouth and giggled.
"I don't understand human language," neighed the horse to the cow, "but did he just call you fat?"
Tommy was puzzled why the cow snorted loudly at him.
After a while, Dr. Dolittle began teaching Tommy how to examine the animals.
"Lucas is very old,"
said Dr. Dolittle, as he patted an aging donkey.
"So you need to be very gentle.
Older animals have problems with their sight, digestion, and joints.
They are also forgetful."
Dr. Dolittle asked Tommy to stand in front of Lucas.
"Now hold up two fingers," he instructed.
Tommy did as he was told.
Dr. Dolittle made some hee-hawing noises.
"How many fingers do you see, Lucas?" he asked.
Lucas blinked once and yawned loudly.
"Pigs," continued the doctor, "are very smart animals.
They know when it is time for their shots.
So you have to distract them."
The doctor snuck up on a pig.
Tommy just stood there watching.
"Come on, Tommy, do something!" encouraged the doctor.
Tommy started to clap his hands and stamp his feet.
"Keep going, Tommy!" urged Dr. Dolittle.
Tommy waved his arms and danced.
"What on earth is that boy doing?" oinked one pig.
"Squeal! Snort!" said another in surprise.
All the pigs got their shots while they watched Tommy dance.
No, it was not easy being a doctor's assistant.
The first few months went by quickly.
Although Tommy was a slow learner, he did not give up easily.
One day, he was having trouble with Gub-Gub.
"Dr. Dolittle?" he called out, holding the pig under his arm.
Dr. Dolittle had his head in the wiff-waff's tank.
So all Dr. Dolittle heard was this: "Duroo Duroo-roo?"
Dr. Dolittle pulled his head out of the tank.
He did not look happy.
"I can't do it," he sighed.
"The wiff-waff isn't able to help me learn the shellfish language."
"But you can't give up!" Tommy pleaded.
The doctor removed his goggles and gloves.
"Well, there is one more hope," he said.
"But we will have to wait and see."
"Doctor, I don't know what's wrong with Gub-Gub."
Tommy handed him the wiggling pig.
The doctor looked Gub-Gub over.
"He looks fine to me," Dr. Dolittle remarked.
"I asked for a piece of cake and look what he gave me!" Gub-Gub cried.
"Yes, Gub-Gub. I told Tommy to give that to you," the doctor said in return.
"No! I hate apples!" pouted the pig.
"You're on a diet.
From now on, only fruits and vegetables for you!" the doctor said sternly.
Just then, Polynesia flew into the room.
She was breathless.
"Oh, doctor! The purple . . ." she gasped.
"Tell me, what is it, Polynesia?" the doctor urged.
Polynesia took a few deep breaths.
"The purple bird of paradise is here.
She brings bad news!"
"Oh, dear, oh, dear!" the doctor frowned.
He dropped Gub-Gub and rushed into the kitchen.
Tommy ran after.
A beautiful purple bird was sitting on the table.
Her head was decorated with a crown of gold that matched her long sweeping tail.
"Miranda!" the doctor shouted.
The beautiful bird dramatically opened one eye.
"Dr. Dolittle!" she moaned.
"Long Arrow has disappeared!"
Dr. Dolittle swayed on his feet and fell into a chair.
"Disappeared? What do you mean?"
Tommy could see that the doctor was very upset.
"Long Arrow doesn't go anywhere without telling us birds," Miranda continued.
"But now he's gone!
Not even a word to the eagles."
"That doesn't make sense!" The doctor shook his head.
"Long Arrow and the eagles are the closest friends!
He always tells them where he is going."
"That is why we fear the worst," the beautiful bird cried.
Dr. Dolittle paced back and forth.
"No. There has got to be some explanation," he kept muttering.
"Where was the last place you saw him?"
"On Spider Monkey Island," replied Miranda.
"Then that is where he must be!" exclaimed the doctor.
"We searched everywhere for the great Indian," said Miranda.
"We flew over the entire island."
"I believe . . . no, I KNOW he is still there!" the doctor said stubbornly.
"We will go to Spider Monkey Island and find Long Arrow!"
At this point, Tommy could take it no longer.
"Excuse me, Dr. Dolittle," interrupted Tommy.
"Please tell me what's going on."
The doctor turned to him and grabbed his shoulders.
"Tommy, Long Arrow is missing and we are going to find him!"
"Who is Long Arrow?" Tommy asked.
"Long Arrow is the greatest naturalist in the world," said the doctor.
"What's a naturalist?" asked Tommy.
"A person who studies nature—plants, animals, insects, everything that lives."
Tommy said, "Can he speak to animals like you?"
"He can communicate with all forms of life.
Long Arrow and I have communicated through Miranda for many years," continued the doctor.
"I recently sent a message asking for his help."
"For what?"
"To understand the language of the shellfish.
But now the great Long Arrow is missing.
And," added Dr. Dolittle firmly,
"it looks as if I will have to go and find my friend!"
"Can I come with you?" Tommy asked excitedly.
He had long dreamed of going off on a voyage with the doctor.
"Yes, but we don't have much time," said Dr. Dolittle.
Tommy could hardly believe it.
He was finally going to travel the world.
There was much to prepare before the voyage.
First, they needed a boat.
A local fisherman named Joe had a boat for sale.
Dr. Dolittle and Tommy looked over the boat.
It was named The Curlew.
The Curlew would be perfect for their journey.
However, there was one problem.
"You need three people to sail this vessel," Joe explained.
"Will you hire two sailors?" Tommy asked the doctor.
Dr. Dolittle shook his head.
"No, I always prefer to sail with friends."
"What about Matthew?" Tommy suggested.
"It may be a difficult journey," Dr. Dolittle stated.
"I think Matthew may be too old."
"Then how about Luke?" Tommy said excitedly.
The doctor stopped in his tracks.
"Yes, that sounds like a good idea, Tommy," he said.
"Let's go, Jip."
Luke lived just outside of Puddleby.
Most everyone was afraid of Luke.
He didn't talk much, nor was he friendly to others.
But Dr. Dolittle and Tommy both knew he had a good heart.
"That's odd," said Dr. Dolittle when they reached Luke's cottage.
"Luke is usually sitting over there"—he pointed to a rocking chair—"and Bob always comes over to greet us."
Bob was Luke's big black scary dog.
He growled and barked at everyone.
But he didn't mind the doctor and Tommy.
And he was friendly with Jip, too.
Tommy looked through the window.
"There's nobody inside," he remarked.
It was very strange indeed.
Jip kept his nose close to the ground.
Suddenly he let out a low growl.
"What is it, Jip?" asked the doctor.
Jip lifted his head and let out a pitiful howl.
He was clearly upset.
Dr. Dolittle kept asking him what the matter was.
But Jip only howled more loudly.
Finally Jip said to the doctor, "I have to go quickly!"
"Jip, what on earth is happening?" Dr. Dolittle shouted.
"I don't have time to explain," he barked.
And with that Jip quickly ran off.
They returned home without Jip.
"Is Jip back yet?"
Dr. Dolittle asked when he walked in the door.
"We thought he was with you," Dab-Dab said, confused.
"What's happened, doctor?" Polynesia asked.
Dr. Dolittle told the others about The Curlew, about Luke, and about Jip's strange behavior.
"Something is definitely wrong," the doctor concluded.
Suddenly they heard loud noises outside.
Tommy ran to the window.
"It's Jip and . . . Bob!"
The two dogs were very upset.
Bob looked so angry that Tommy felt afraid to get near him.
Only Dr. Dolittle was brave enough to approach.
"Jip! Bob! Calm down!" he ordered.
The dogs obeyed.
"Now," continued the doctor, "tell me what happened."
"Luke is a good man.
He didn't do it," Bob barked over and over again.
"Didn't do what?" asked Dr. Dolittle.
"He didn't kill that man!" howled Bob.
Tommy took another step back.
"Kill who, Bob?" the doctor demanded to know.
"That man fell in the well," wailed Bob.
"Where is Luke now?" asked Dr. Dolittle.
"In jail," Jip answered.
"We must go and see him," said the doctor, firmly.
With the help of Dr. Dolittle and Polynesia, Tommy understood what had happened.
"I can't believe Luke would harm anyone, doctor," cried Tommy.
"Nor can I, Tommy," said the doctor gravely.
"That's why we must go and see Luke."
Luke was being held in a dark, damp cell.
Bob started to whine sadly when he saw his master.
Dr. Dolittle called out Luke's name several times, but he didn't respond.
"Luke!" he called again.
Finally, Luke lifted his head.
"We're here to help you, Luke," said the doctor.
Luke shook his head.
"I killed him. There's nothing you can do."
Dr. Dolittle and Tommy looked at each other with concern.
Bob began barking wildly.
"That's not true! That's not true!"
Dr. Dolittle knelt down beside Bob.
"Did you see what happened?" he asked.
Bob let out a loud bark. "Yes!"
The doctor sat talking with Bob for a few minutes.
Finally, he stood up and said, "I have a plan.
I don't know if it's going to work, but I will do my best."
"What for, doctor?
No one is going to believe you," said Luke.
"And the trial is about to begin."
"But they will believe the witness," Dr. Dolittle assured him.
"Witness? There were no witnesses," Luke exclaimed.
"Yes, there was," said Dr. Dolittle.
"Bob saw what happened."
A few hours later, Luke's trial began.
It wasn't going well for Luke.
The man called the prosecutor had a long nose.
He kept pointing a finger at Luke and accusing him of many awful things.
Then he called for a man named Mendoza to stand up.
Mendoza explained that he, Luke, and another man named Boggs were partners.
"What kind of partners?" asked the prosecutor.
"We were looking for gold," Mendoza answered.
"Finally one day, we hit it big!"
Mendoza rubbed his hands greedily and licked his lips.
Bob growled dangerously.
"But what happened?" the prosecutor asked.
"That man," Mendoza pointed to Luke, "wanted the gold for himself.
So he killed Boggs.
He would have killed me, but I escaped."
Bob jumped up and barked loudly.
"Quiet! Silence!" shouted the judge.
Luke's lawyer stood up.
"Your honor, I would like to call Dr. Dolittle."
"Dr. Dolittle? The animal doctor?" the judge asked in surprise.
"Yes, Your Honor," replied Luke's lawyer.
"He is going to speak on behalf of the witness, Luke's dog Bob."
At that, the courtroom exploded with loud laughter.
Dr. Dolittle stood before the judge.
"Can you really speak to animals?" the judge asked.
"Yes, Your Honor," confirmed the doctor.
"That's impossible," whispered some people in the courtroom.
"He can! He cured my horse," said a man beside them.
"This is an outrage!" protested the prosecutor.
The judge sat silent for a moment or two.
"You must prove that you can talk with animals.
Then I will allow you to speak on behalf of Bob," he finally said.
He motioned to a guard.
The guard went out and came back with the judge's dog.
The judge's dog was even bigger than Bob.
He sat in the witness box and growled, showing sharp white teeth.
"Now, Doctor," said the judge, "this is Sweetie." Everyone giggled.
"Only Sweetie and I know what I had for dinner last night.
Ask him what I ate, Doctor."
Dr. Dolittle approached Sweetie and began to make dog noises.
"What on earth is he doing?" a large woman whispered.
"It's a trick!
How can a man speak to animals?" a man said nastily.
Dr. Dolittle glanced at the judge and began to giggle.
He continued talking with Sweetie.
"What's taking so long?" the judge asked impatiently.
"Oh, sorry, Your Honor.
Sweetie was telling me what you did after supper," chuckled the doctor.
"Never mind that," the judge snapped.
"What did I have for dinner?"
"You had lamb chops, potatoes, and a glass of wine," the doctor smiled, "and then you left the house and . . ."
The judge's eyes grew very wide.
Interrupting, he said quickly, "Very well.
Bob is allowed as a witness."
Luke's trial went more smoothly after that.
Of course, the prosecutor was not happy.
He objected loudly, but the judge shut him up.
Bob got on the witness stand and told everyone what really happened.
Luke, Boggs, and Mendoza had been looking for gold.
One day, Luke came across a large rock that turned out to be gold.
When he showed it to Boggs and Mendoza, they wanted the gold for themselves.
The next day, Boggs accidentally dropped his hat in the well.
"Let me down the well," he said to Luke.
So Boggs climbed into the bucket while Luke held tightly to the rope.
At that point Mendoza walked by.
"Aha, this is my chance!" he said to himself.
He pulled out a gun and crept quietly toward Luke.
Bob tried to warn his master.
But all Luke's attention was on watching Boggs and holding the rope tight.
Mendoza got closer and closer.
Bob barked and barked, but Luke didn't hear.
Bob knew Luke's life was in danger!
So he opened his jaw and bit down hard on Luke's leg.
Luke shouted in pain and let go of the rope.
"Bad dog! Bad dog!" Luke scolded Bob.
Mendoza quickly hid his gun.
"What happened?" he asked innocently.
They both looked down the well.
Boggs was gone.
Luke was upset, but Mendoza was sly.
"If you don't give me the gold," he said, "I will tell everyone that you killed Boggs on purpose."
So Luke gave the gold to Mendoza.
The courtroom was silent.
Some people even began crying.
"Poor Luke," they said, "it wasn't his fault!"
Even the judge wiped a tear from his eye.
The next day, Luke stood before the judge.
"You are not guilty," he declared.
Everyone jumped up and clapped loudly.
Dr. Dolittle and Tommy ran up to Luke.
He smiled at them and said simply, "Thank you."
Luke's trial delayed their trip for a few days, so they were busier than ever.
"You were incredible," Tommy said with awe.
"No, Tommy, Bob was the one who saved Luke," the doctor corrected.
"He was very loyal and brave."
A man wearing clean clothes and a big smile walked up to them.
"Dr. Dolittle?" he called out.
Tommy could not believe his eyes.
It was Luke!
He looked completely different.
Luke and Dr. Dolittle spoke for a few minutes.
"I'm very sorry, but I won't be able to join you on your voyage," Luke said.
"That's quite all right," replied the doctor.
"But I do want to give you something," said Luke.
Luke let out a loud whistle.
Bob, Jip, and Sweetie arrived, pulling a large wagon.
Dr. Dolittle uncovered the wagon.
It was filled with all kinds of food.
"Oh, Luke! Just what we need for our trip!" the doctor exclaimed.
"Mendoza had to return my gold rock," Luke said shyly.
"So now I have lots of money."
Just then Polynesia came by with an unexpected visitor.
"Dr. Dolittle!" she cried out.
"Guess who I met?"
Dr. Dolittle rubbed his eyes.
He couldn't believe what he was seeing.
"Is that the prince of Jolliginki?" he said.
It was indeed.
Years ago, the African prince had helped Dr. Dolittle escape from his father's prison.
"I am a university student now," explained the prince.
"When I heard you were living here, I had to come and see you."
"Well, I'm so glad you did," said the doctor.
They spoke a while about the prince's family.
Suddenly the doctor asked, "Would you like to travel with us?"
The prince answered immediately, "I would be delighted!
I am on my summer holidays at the moment."
"That's wonderful!" the doctor said.
"Now we're ready for our voyage!"
"But, Doctor," interrupted Tommy, "we need three people to sail The Curlew.
Who is the third man?"
"You are, Tommy," said the doctor, and he winked.
At last the voyage was about to begin.
"There!" exclaimed the doctor, "I think we're ready to sail!"
Tommy rubbed his hands together with excitement.
When he saw his crying mother, he turned his back.
Tommy did not want her to see how excited he was to leave.
"Why can't we come with you, Dr. Dolittle!" Gub-Gub snorted loudly.
"It's not fair!" barked Jip angrily.
"I can cook for you," quacked Dab-Dab.
"Hmm, what time is it?" yawned a sleepy Too-Too.
Dr. Dolittle knelt down before them.
"I wish all of you could come," he said kindly, "but the boat is too small.
"Besides," he continued, "who is going to take care of the house and garden?"
The animals hung their heads low.
They really wanted to go on this voyage with the doctor.
"Am I late?" a voice shouted from a distance.
Tommy squinted his eyes.
"Oh!" he said, "it's the prince."
The prince wore a white sailor suit and hat.
He carried two very large suitcases.
"Your Highness," Dr. Dolittle began.
The prince smiled broadly.
"On this voyage I am not a prince.
I'm a sailor," he said.
"You may call me . . ."—he paused—"Charles."
"Okay Charles," said Dr. Dolittle.
"Er...Charles," he continued, chuckling, "I'm afraid you can't bring both those bags."
"Why not?" the prince asked.
"We don't have enough room," Dr. Dolittle replied.
"But I need all my books," said Charles, "and my rock collection, my shoes, my cooking spices, my . . ."
But in the end, Charles had to leave everything behind.
Dr. Dolittle clapped his hands.
"Well, we should get going."
Tommy hugged his parents.
"Remember to brush your teeth every morning," sobbed his mother.
"Here," his father said, "I made these for you."
He handed Tommy a brand new pair of shoes.
"I will wear them every day," Tommy promised.
Dr. Dolittle looked around.
"That's odd," he said.
"Where did everyone go?"
The animals were nowhere to be seen.
"I saw them here a minute ago," said Tommy.
"They must have gone home because they were too upset," said the doctor.
Then he cupped his hands and shouted:
"All aboard on The Curlew!"
As they left Puddleby, Tommy looked over the map.
"I can't find Spider Monkey Island," he said.
"Of course not," answered the doctor.
"What do you mean?" asked Tommy.
"Spider Monkey Island is a floating island!" replied the doctor.
"A floating island?" Tommy cried out.
"Then how are we going to find it?"
"Don't worry," said the doctor, "Miranda told us where to look."
"And the whales and eagles will tell us how to get there," Polynesia added.
Tommy put the map down.
"I guess we won't need this," he said.
"Dr. Dolittle!" Charles ran toward them.
The doctor turned to look at him.
"I was making sandwiches for our lunch," said Charles, "when I discovered something interesting."
He motioned for them to follow.
Charles put a finger to his lips and tiptoed into the kitchen.
Everyone followed him quietly.
"Now watch this," he whispered.
Charles made a large sandwich and placed it on the table.
The cupboard door opened and something snatched the sandwich off the table.
Dr. Dolittle quietly went to the cupboard and swung the door open.
"Gub-Gub!" the doctor shouted.
The pig began to cry.
"I'm sorry, Dr. Dolittle!
Jip made me do it."
A deep growling sound came from a sack of potatoes.
Tommy went over and opened it.
"Sorry, Doctor," Jip barked, from inside the bag.
"Well, it looks as if we have a few uninvited guests!" the doctor remarked.
"Uh, Doctor," Tommy pointed to a large barrel.
"I think that barrel just coughed."
Dr. Dolittle opened the lid and found old Matthew covered in flour.
"Ahhh," muttered Matthew wiped his nose. "Ahhh-chooooo!"
Dr. Dolittle called a meeting with all the stowaways.
"I am very disappointed in you, Jip," he scolded.
"And you, too, Gub-Gub!"
"We only wanted to go with you, Dr. Dolittle," the pig cried.
"And I wanted to be part of your adventures," interrupted Matthew.
Dr. Dolittle shook his head.
"I'm afraid this trip is not an adventure, but a rescue mission."
"To rescue whom?" asked Matthew.
But the doctor did not explain.
"Tommy," he said instead, "bring me the map."
Tommy returned with the map.
"Aha," said the doctor after a while,
"Capa Blanca Islands."
Everyone waited quietly for the doctor to continue.
"We can stop there and drop off the stowaways," he said.
Dr. Dolittle turned the boat toward the north.
"Is it very far from here?" Tommy asked.
"Not too far," the doctor replied.
"Polynesia!" he called, "how is the water temperature?"
Polynesia pulled up her tail.
At the end of her tail was a long piece of string.
And tied to the end of the string was a thermometer.
"Brrr!" she shivered. "The water feels cold."
Polynesia held the thermometer close to her face.
"I must be getting old," she sighed.
"I can't see what it says."
Tommy helped her read the thermometer.
"It looks okay," said Tommy.
"Good," said Dr. Dolittle.
"If the water temperature is very cold, there might be icebergs nearby."
At that moment, there was a loud thump followed by a cracking noise.
"The thermometer must be broken!" cried Polynesia.
"Dr. Dolittle! Be careful!" shouted Tommy.
But it was too late.
Dr. Dolittle lost control of the wheel and fell.
Tommy ran over to Dr. Dolittle to help him up.
"Grab the wheel, Tommy!" the doctor shouted.
Tommy tried but it was too heavy.
"I can't see the iceberg, Doctor!" he gasped.
"It must be underwater," Dr. Dolittle replied.
There was another cracking sound and Tommy saw water leaking into the boat.
Meanwhile, there was trouble in the kitchen.
"Hurry, Chip!" yelled Charles.
"My name is Jip! Not Chip!" barked the dog.
But of course Charles could not understand animal language.
"Cover the holes with the potato sacks!" he cried.
They blocked the water with the sacks.
Soon the water seeped through the potatoes.
"What should we do?" cried Charles.
"I have an idea!" oinked Gub-Gub.
But of course the humans only heard snorting sounds.
"Use the flour!
Like making bread!" the pig cried.
"What are you talking about?" barked Jip.
"I saw Dab-Dab do it," the pig explained.
Gub-Gub opened the lid of one barrel.
"What on earth is that pig doing?" shouted Matthew.
He did not have fond memories of flour barrels.
Gub-Gub pushed the barrel over.
Flour came spilling out.
Then, using a broom, he pushed it toward the holes.
As the flour absorbed the water, it became sticky and thick.
It turned into dough.
The dough plugged the holes.
"What a clever pig!" said Charles.
Together they began emptying all the flour barrels.
Soon the kitchen looked like a giant oven filled with dough.
The water stopped leaking into the boat.
"That should hold us till we get to land," said Matthew.
"I'm quite impressed,"
Charles said as he handed Gub-Gub another biscuit.
Gub-Gub snorted loudly.
After a while the boat was under control again.
"What happened?" asked Tommy.
"I think it must have been a rock," replied the doctor.
"The boat's been damaged, especially in the kitchen," said Charles.
"And we have no more flour," added Matthew, "and the potatoes are spoiled."
Everyone's heart felt heavy.
But soon their spirits lifted.
"Land ho!" Polynesia called from the mast.
They all stood up to look.
Indeed, land was within sight.
"We'll get our boat fixed," said the doctor happily, "and get some more food.
Then we'll be on our way to Spider Monkey Island."
When they reached land, Dr. Dolittle bought another boat from a fisherman.
The boat was not as nice as The Curlew.
It was not as big either.
But Dr. Dolittle was satisfied.
"Tell me, sir, what is this island called?" Dr. Dolittle asked the fisherman.
"You're on Capa Blanca Island!" said the old man.
Dr. Dolittle looked at his friends and winked.
"We made it after all," he smiled.
"You're just in time, too," said the fisherman.
"For what?" asked Tommy.
"For the bullfight!
It's the greatest show on earth!" the fisherman explained.
Dr. Dolittle's eyes grew dark and his forehead wrinkled.
"When does this bullfight begin?"
the doctor asked in a low, angry voice.
Tommy had never seen the doctor so upset.
"This afternoon," replied the fisherman.
"And the Great Pepito will bravely fight those ferocious beasts!"
Dr. Dolittle and the others walked in silence toward a large ship.
The doctor was holding a ticket.
"Matthew," he said, "This ship is going to England.
Take Jip and Gub-Gub back home for me, please."
The animals, of course, did not want to go back.
"But what about the bullfight?" howled Jip.
"We have to put a stop to it!"
"I'll take care of that, Jip," the doctor replied sternly.
"Besides, the new boat is too small for all of us."
The ship's horn blew.
Dr. Dolittle wiped a tear from his eye as he waved good-bye.
"We'll be seeing them soon," Polynesia said.
They watched as the ship pulled away.
Charles looked around and said, "Doctor, we should get our food for the voyage soon."
The market was closing early for the bullfight.
Dr. Dolittle shook his head sadly.
"We have no money left," he said.
"But how can that be?" asked Tommy.
"I bought the boat," the doctor explained.
"Then I used the last of the money to buy tickets for Matthew, Jip, and Gub-Gub."
Although Tommy was adventurous, the thought of having no money scared him.
"Don't worry, child," whispered Polynesia.
"The doctor will take care of it.
He always does."
It was the first time Tommy wished he were back home in Puddleby.
All around Capa Blanca Island, excitement buzzed in the air.
Everyone was going to the bullfight.
Tommy finally had the courage to ask the doctor:
"What is a bullfight?"
The doctor's face turned red.
"A bullfight," he explained angrily, "is a stupid, crazy, and dangerous business.
Some call it a sport.
Some say it is art.
But I say it is murder—murder of a poor innocent animal!"
Dr. Dolittle's lips trembled and he paused.
Finally he went on.
"First the bull is teased and made angry.
Then the bull is let out and chased around the village.
After he is tired out, he is led back into the arena and killed!"
"By who?" Tommy interrupted.
"The matador—that's the bullfighter.
There he is!" Dr. Dolittle pointed.
A man wearing a gold outfit and funny black hat walked down the middle of the street.
People cheered and called out, "The Great Pepito!"
Dr. Dolittle looked even angrier.
"Come on, Tommy," he said.
"I have a plan."
Don Enrique was the richest man on the island.
His best friend, Don Carlo, was the mayor of Capa Blanca.
Dr. Dolittle approached the two men and said,
"I would like to make a proposal."
"What is it?" asked the mayor.
"I am a better bullfighter than that man with the funny hat," the doctor said bravely.
"He is Pepito the Great!" shouted Don Enrique.
"The greatest bullfighter on the island!"
"Whoever he is," the doctor continued, "I am better than he is."
"You?" laughed the men.
"How can you be better than our greatest bullfighter?"
"For one thing, I can make the bulls do silly tricks," said the doctor.
This made the men laugh harder.
Dr. Dolittle was getting impatient.
"I will prove it, if you grant me one wish," he announced.
"What is your wish, sir?"
the mayor asked between tears of laughter.
"There will be no more bullfighting in Capa Blanca!" the doctor said firmly.
Tommy was really worried about Dr. Dolittle.
"Have you ever fought a bull before?" he asked.
"Of course not, Tommy," the doctor replied.
"I would never fight an animal."
Now Tommy was truly afraid.
The black bulls were big, strong, and very angry.
They kicked out their hind legs and snorted loudly.
"Stay here," Dr. Dolittle instructed Tommy.
Then he opened the bull pen and went inside.
Tommy covered his eyes with his hands.
"Please be careful," he cried to the doctor.
The bulls did not like humans.
They made a circle around the doctor and glared at him.
"What does this fool want?" snorted one.
"I'm going to kick him out,"
said another, lowering his sharp horns.
"That's not very nice!" the doctor said to them.
The bulls blinked their eyes in surprise.
"You can speak our language?" one said.
"Of course! Now, I have to explain quickly," the doctor said.
"Are you Dr. Dolittle?" another said in a trembling voice.
"Yes, yes, I am," the doctor said.
"We've heard so many wonderful things about you!" they cried out happily.
"Thank you," the doctor said.
"But please listen to me!
We don't have much time."
The bulls all started talking at once.
They wanted to know how the doctor had learned their language.
"Stop!" the largest bull said.
"Let the doctor speak!"
So Dr. Dolittle told them his plan.
Meanwhile, Polynesia had an idea of her own.
She and Charles went back to Don Enrique.
"What do you want now?" he shouted rudely.
Polynesia whispered in Charles' ear.
"We'd like to place a small bet," he said.
Don Enrique liked bets.
That's how he had become so rich.
"How much do you want to bet and on whom?" he asked.
"Two thousand gold coins on John Dolittle," said Charles.
"That man couldn't fight flies!" roared Don Enrique.
"He thinks he is better than the Great Pepito!"
"I have changed my mind," said Charles.
"I knew you would," laughed Don Enrique.
"I want to raise my bet to three thousand on Dolittle," Charles said.
Don Enrique slapped his knee.
"You are going to make me even richer," he said.
He and Charles shook hands.
The bet was made.
Inside the arena, the crowds shouted loudly for the fight to begin.
The mayor stood up and shouted, "Ladies and Gentlemen!
May I present the greatest fighter of all—Pepito!"
Tommy watched Pepito come out, holding a red cloak.
A large bull was let out of the pen.
The bull turned around and ran toward Pepito.
Pepito swung his cloak and jumped away.
The people screamed in delight and called out his name.
After a little while, it was Dr. Dolittle's turn.
"And now, John Dolittle," the mayor said quickly.
People booed and hissed.
The doctor walked to the middle of the arena.
An even bigger, angrier bull was let out.
He threw his head back and snorted loudly.
Some women screamed in fear.
Dr. Dolittle held up his hands, but the bull began to charge.
When the bull got close, the doctor clapped his hands once.
The huge animal stopped and dropped to his knees.
Then the doctor climbed onto its back.
The audience held its breath.
Suddenly the doctor grabbed the bull's horns and did a handstand.
Dr. Dolittle jumped off and the bull stood up again.
"How was that?" whispered the bull.
"You were brilliant," answered the doctor.
"Now, one last thing."
The doctor put out his hand and twirled it in a circle, faster and faster.
The bull stood on its hind legs and danced around.
Then it fell to the ground with a loud thump.
The people went crazy.
"The Great Dolittle!" they screamed.
Dr. Dolittle looked at the mayor.
The mayor was wiping tears from his eyes.
"Ladies and Gentlemen," he cried.
"I have sad news.
This was our last bullfight."
The crowds shouted angrily.
The bull opened one eye and smiled at the doctor.
"Thank you," he said.
After the bullfight, Polynesia and Charles collected the money from Don Enrique.
They found a woman opening up her shop again.
"Quickly, Charles!" said Polynesia.
"We must buy everything she has and get it to our boat."
"What's the hurry?" Charles asked.
"Soon the people will be angry at Dr. Dolittle," she replied.
"He has stopped all bullfights."
Charles carried food and supplies back and forth to the boat.
Soon Tommy came along and helped him.
"Where is the doctor?" whispered Charles.
"Hiding on the boat.
The people are looking for him," Tommy answered.
An angry mob appeared in the distance.
"Look! That's Dolittle's people!
Get them!" they yelled.
Charles and Tommy ran as fast as they could.
"Doctor! Get the boat started!" shouted Charles.
Dr. Dolittle came out of his hiding place.
He ran to the wheel and started the boat.
Charles and Tommy jumped on.
They were off to sea again.
The next few weeks were filled with beautiful warm weather.
Tommy was so glad to leave Capa Blanca.
"Will the mayor keep his promise never to have bullfights again?" Tommy asked.
"Yes," answered the doctor.
"That's why the people were so angry."
"Were you at all afraid of the bulls, Dr. Dolittle?" asked Charles.
Dr. Dolittle shook his head.
"Animals never hurt others unless they are hurt first," he said.
"They're very different from humans that way."
Then the doctor pulled up his net and shouted loudly, "A fidgit! I got a fidgit!"
Tommy had never heard of a fidgit.
It looked like a plain little silver fish to him.
"This," Dr. Dolittle pointed excitedly, "will help me understand the shellfish language."
"Do fidgits speak shellfish?" asked Tommy.
"No, but they are relatives of gorfins," explained the doctor.
"Gorfins are cousins of the crabs, who speak shellfish!"
Tommy did not understand at all.
Dr. Dolittle worked hard into the night.
Tommy stayed close by in case the doctor needed him.
Finally, the doctor poked his head out of the tank.
"Extraordinary," he remarked.
Tommy rubbed his eyes sleepily.
"What is it, Doctor?" he asked.
The doctor removed his goggles.
"I want you to listen," he said, "and tell me what you hear."
Tommy put the goggles on and stuck his head into the water.
The tiny fish swam around and around making no sound.
Suddenly Tommy heard a faint noise.
He listened more carefully.
It sounded like: "Don tappan dee gloss."
Tommy pulled his head out.
"Doctor," he gasped, "I think I know what it said."
"What?" asked Dr. Dolittle.
"Don't tap on the glass!" Tommy jumped up and down.
"I understood his language!"
Dr. Dolittle turned pink.
"Um, Tommy," he coughed, "I believe that fidgit is speaking English."
Tommy was very disappointed.
He was never going to learn animal talk.
"But see? If a fidgit can learn to speak human language, then surely we can speak theirs," the doctor reassured him.
Dr. Dolittle pulled out a notepad.
"Here is what I recorded from the fidgit so far."
He began to read.
"'Very rare. Do not smoke.
Please be quiet. Don't tap on the glass.'"
Dr. Dolittle scratched his head.
"I believe this little fish escaped from an aquarium!"
Dr. Dolittle and Tommy listened, recorded, and tried to speak to the fidgit all night.
Yes, it had escaped from an aquarium.
That's where it learned to speak human talk.
"Tommy!" cried the doctor, sticking his head out of the tank.
"The fidgit has something to say!"
They both put their faces back into the water and waited.
"Thank you for coming to see my show," the little fish began.
Tommy started to giggle, which made bubbles under the water.
"Please do not smoke.
Do not tap on the glass," the fidgit continued.
"And if you want to learn shellfish language, seek the great glass sea snail."
"Er, who is that?" asked the doctor.
"He is the oldest living creature in the world," the fidgit replied.
"A snail that is as big as a house."
"Where can we find him?" asked Tommy.
"The snail lives only in one place," the fidgit answered.
"Find Spider Monkey Island and you will find him."
Dr. Dolittle had to let the fish go.
"I wanted to take him back to Puddleby," the doctor said,
"but he is so much happier in his own water world."
Everyone nodded in agreement.
"Just look how beautiful and calm the waters are," sighed Charles.
"Look at that silly bird!"
Tommy stood up and pointed.
A bird was coming toward them, but it couldn't seem to fly straight.
Everyone except Polynesia laughed.
"Dr. Dolittle," she said seriously,
"I think it's Miranda."
"Miranda?" exclaimed the doctor.
"What is she doing here?"
As the bird approached, they recognized the purple bird of paradise.
"Oh," Miranda gasped as she fell onto the boat.
"Miranda! Are you all right?" the doctor called out.
"Yes," she finally said.
"I was looking for you for weeks!
But I couldn't find The Curlew anywhere!"
"Yes, er, well . . . we had to change boats," stammered the doctor.
"I bring bad news," she continued.
"A storm, a big storm, is coming."
Tommy looked up at the clear sunny sky.
It certainly didn't look as if a storm were coming.
"It's not too late to turn back, Dr. Dolittle," Miranda said.
The doctor shook his head.
She tried again.
"I wish you would."
"We are going to Spider Monkey Island," the doctor said firmly.
"Then be very careful, Doctor," she said sadly.
Miranda shook her wings and flew away.
Everyone watched her disappear into the blue sky.
That night Miranda's words came true.
"Tommy! Charles! Wake up!"
Dr. Dolittle's voice sounded from the dark.
Tommy turned the lamp on.
"I need you on the deck!" the doctor said urgently.
"The storm is here."
Dr. Dolittle stood by the wheel trying to turn it to the right.
But the wind kept pushing the boat to the left.
"The sails," Dr. Dolittle shouted loudly.
"Take the sails down!"
Polynesia was untying the ropes with her beak.
"Where is Charles?" she screeched.
"Still asleep!" Tommy yelled back.
Polynesia was very upset.
She flew down to the cabin to wake Charles up.
"Get up! Get up!" she yelled.
She pecked him on the nose and forehead.
And she pulled his ears─hard!
"Ouch!" He jumped up out of bed.
The wind tossed the boat this way and that.
The wheel spun out of control, knocking Dr. Dolittle to the floor.
As for poor Tommy, he could not get the sails off by himself.
In fact, the wind was so strong that it lifted him off his feet!
"Hang on tightly!" Dr. Dolittle shouted.
Charles ran onto the deck.
The rain beat against his face.
"That hurts more than Polynesia's pecking!" he cried.
Charles was a big strong man, but even he could not get the sails down.
"The wind is blowing too hard," he yelled.
Tommy was never so frightened in his whole life.
But he knew he must help Charles.
"The sail is stuck!" Polynesia was saying to Charles.
"Tommy! Can you climb up the mast?" she shouted.
Tommy looked up.
The mast was awfully high up.
But he knew he had to do it.
"Yes," he answered.
Then he started to climb up the thick pole.
Tommy reached the top.
One of the sails was caught between the ropes.
That's why they weren't able to pull the sails down.
Tommy used all his strength and pulled the sail loose.
As it fell onto the boat, he heard Charles and Polynesia yelling up at him.
Tommy turned his head and saw a huge wave coming toward him.
There was no time to climb down.
He closed his eyes and held tightly to the mast.
He thought about his mother and father in Puddleby.
Then everything went black.
The storm ended just as quickly as it began—almost as if it had never happened.
The next day was sunny, beautiful, and calm once again.
The boat, however, did not survive the wind and rain.
When Tommy opened his eyes, he found himself still holding onto the mast.
There were pieces of wood everywhere.
Tommy even saw the boat's wheel floating by.
But there were no signs of Dr. Dolittle, Charles, or Polynesia.
He was all alone.
"I will not cry,"
Tommy said as he wiped away his tears.
"They are alive, I know it!"
Tommy tried to think of happy thoughts.
"Someone will find me.
I will be together with my friends again," he said aloud.
At that moment, Tommy looked into the water and screamed.
There were two scary sharks swimming around him.
"Go away, please," he whispered.
One shark poked his head out of the water.
"He doesn't look too good," he said to his friend.
The other came out of the water and looked at Tommy.
"Not much meat on him, is there?"
"Did you find anything else around?
Something tastier?" the first shark licked its lips.
"Nope. This small human is the only thing I can see," the second one said.
Tommy wished he could speak their language.
He decided to use what he had already learned.
"Oink, quack, hee-haw, woof-woof," he said.
The sharks looked confused.
"What's he doing?" one asked.
"Don't ask me," said the other.
"I can never understand these humans."
"Shall we eat him or not?"
But before they could decide, a long, horrible screeching sound was heard.
Tommy and the sharks looked up.
"Polynesia!" cried Tommy joyfully.
She swooped down and started to bite the sharks' noses.
"Shame on you!
Trying to eat a helpless boy!" she scolded them.
"That hurts!" "Aw!" the sharks cried and dived back into the water.
Tommy was so happy to see his friend.
He could not stop crying.
"Now, now, Tommy," said the parrot, comforting him.
"What about the doctor? Charles?" Tommy sobbed.
"We're all safe."
Polynesia explained everything that had happened.
"The doctor and Charles are on land, waiting for you.
So we should go to them as soon as possible."
"But how?" asked Tommy.
"I don't have anything to row with."
"We don't need oars," she replied.
"Our friends will help us."
Tommy suddenly felt the mast gliding along in the water.
"Hold on tight," Polynesia called out.
Tommy turned around to see two beautiful dolphins.
They were using their long noses to push the mast forward.
Tommy wanted to reach out and touch their smooth, shiny skin.
"Everything okay?" Polynesia called out to the dolphins.
"It certainly is!
He's light as a feather!" one replied.
"Not like Dr. Dolittle and that other man," called out the other.
"Now that was heavy!"
The dolphins laughed out cheerfully.
"Yes, Dr. Dolittle told me he'd put on some weight," laughed Tommy.
Polynesia stared at Tommy.
The dolphins stopped pushing and poked their heads out of the water.
Tommy did not know why everyone was looking at him.
"Did I say something wrong?" he asked shyly.
"Tommy," Polynesia said finally,
"just now, you understood our language and spoke it."
"What?" Tommy shook his head in confusion.
He thought about what had just happened.
Yes, he clearly understood what the dolphins said.
"Oh, my!" he exclaimed.
"I can speak! I can speak!"
Soon, Tommy saw the island ahead.
Dr. Dolittle and Charles were waving their hands excitedly.
Tommy did not know what made him happier:
seeing his friends again or finally being able to speak animal language.
He decided that both things made him equally happy.
They ate a meal of fresh fruits, and Tommy told Dr. Dolittle about the dolphins.
"How exciting!" the doctor exclaimed.
"I knew you could do it!"
"I still have so much to learn," Tommy said humbly.
The island was large with high, rocky mountains in the middle.
No one knew where they were.
"All our maps were swept away in that storm," said the doctor.
"But at least I saved this,"
he said as he held up his black medicine bag.
"And these." From inside the bag he pulled out his notebooks.
Tommy suddenly felt sad that he didn't have any of his things.
Then the doctor surprised him.
"These are yours, I think."
The doctor held up the shoes Tommy's father had given him.
"Oh, thank you, Dr. Dolittle!" Tommy cried.
"And this is yours, I believe."
The doctor gave Charles a thick book.
"How wonderful you are," Charles exclaimed, hugging him.
Tommy got up to get another piece of fruit.
He suddenly got the feeling that he was being watched.
Sounds came from the trees.
"Uh, Doctor?" he called out softly.
Just then, an entire tribe of island men came out of the trees.
Tommy ran to Dr. Dolittle and Charles.
Dr. Dolittle jumped up in delight.
"So there are people living here!
How wonderful!" he cried out.
He walked toward the natives, his arms spread wide and a big smile on his face.
But the men did not smile back.
They raised their swords in the air.
Hiding behind Charles, Tommy observed the island natives.
All of them wore animal skins.
Most of them were tall and had a white mark on their forehead.
The man in the middle, however, was short and looked scary.
He had a red mark on each cheek.
Tommy guessed that he was their chief.
Dr. Dolittle tried to communicate with them.
"We are friends," he said slowly.
The natives did not show any response.
Instead, they took a step forward and pointed their swords at the doctor.
"I don't think they understand," Charles said.
Suddenly, from behind came a loud shout.
A young boy around Tommy's age ran out and said something to the short man.
Then he spoke a few words to his men.
After giving the doctor a long stare, they quietly went back into the trees.
"That's not a very warm welcome, is it?" remarked Charles.
"They don't understand why we are here," the doctor said.
"Why did they leave like that?" wondered Tommy.
"Well," said Polynesia, "I think we should find a way off this island."
As everyone thought about Polynesia's words, they heard a loud buzzing sound.
It wasn't a bee, because they couldn't see anything flying around.
"Look! Over there!"
Tommy pointed to a branch of a tree.
Crawling along it was a large insect.
Dr. Dolittle went to examine it.
"I can't believe it!" he said.
"It's a jabizri!"
"A what?" asked Charles as he stepped back.
The jabizri was pale blue on the underside but black with large red spots on its back.
It was a beautiful insect.
"Well, that's interesting," the doctor said.
"There is something tied to it."
A thin leaf was wrapped around its leg.
It was tied tightly with spider web.
Dr. Dolittle carefully held the insect and untangled the web.
After giving the jabizri to Tommy, the doctor spread the leaf out on his hand.
The leaf was covered in drawings, signs, and symbols.
One of them showed three men inside a mountain.
A large rock covered the entrance.
"This is a message for help," the doctor said.
Then he let out a gasp.
"Look, Tommy!" he pointed.
At the bottom was a drawing of a spider crawling across a monkey's head.
"Spider Monkey Island!"
Tommy and the doctor shouted at the same time.
"We're on Spider Monkey Island!"
While Dr. Dolittle studied the leaf, Tommy and Charles picked more fruit.
"The men in the mountains will be hungry," said Charles.
"They will want something to eat."
"Good thinking, Charles!"
Dr. Dolittle patted him on the shoulder.
Then the doctor let out such a cry that Tommy dropped two pieces of fruit.
"It's Long Arrow!" he shouted.
"Where?" Charles looked around.
"No, here! He's here!"
said Dr. Dolittle as he pointed to the leaf.
Everyone stood around the doctor.
"How do you know?" asked Tommy.
The doctor pointed to one drawing.
Tommy couldn't tell what it was.
"This is an eagle's nest," Dr. Dolittle explained.
"Inside the nest is a man.
That's Long Arrow.
Everyone knows he is close friends with the eagles."
Tommy didn't know that.
The doctor stood up and said,
"We have no time to waste!
Long Arrow is in danger.
He needs our help."
"It looks like he's up there."
Charles pointed to the mountains.
"But where? The mountains are so big!" said Tommy.
Again the doctor showed him the leaf drawing.
"See the mountain top?
It looks like a hawk's head.
That's where they are!" he said.
Without another word, everyone started running toward the mountains.
"Wait! Let's take the jabizri!" the doctor called out suddenly.
"Here it is," said Tommy.
Tommy held up a fruit that looked like an orange.
He had made a small cut on top and scraped out all the flesh.
He placed the insect inside and put the cut out part back in place—like a lid.
The doctor smiled at him.
"What a clever boy you are!" he said.
Climbing up the mountain was long and difficult.
Tommy's legs were shaking so badly that he wanted to sit down and rest.
But Long Arrow and his men needed them.
They had to go on.
After many hours, Dr. Dolittle and the others finally made it to the top.
"Look for the hawk's head," said Dr. Dolittle.
They looked and looked but saw nothing like a hawk's head.
"Doctor," Polynesia said carefully, "maybe we should try again tomorrow.
It's getting dark."
"We will find Long Arrow tonight," Dr. Dolittle said firmly.
No one spoke for a while.
Then Dr. Dolittle snapped his fingers.
"That's it!" he shouted.
"Tommy! Let the jabizri go."
Tommy wanted to keep the beautiful insect as a pet.
"The jabizri will lead us to Long Arrow," said the doctor.
So Tommy took the lid off the fruit and watched as the jabizri crawled out.
"Keep your eye on it," instructed the doctor.
The jabizri stretched its six legs then walked around in a circle three times.
"What's it doing?" Charles cried impatiently.
"The poor thing is stretching," said Polynesia.
"It was trapped in that fruit for a very long time."
Finally the jabizri began to move.
Dr. Dolittle and the others followed it downward.
It led them to one side of the mountain.
Then the jabizri disappeared inside a crack.
"Now what do we do?" moaned Charles.
But the doctor was busy examining the crack in the mountain.
"This looks like an entrance," Dr. Dolittle said.
"Dr. Dolittle!" Tommy cried excitedly as he pointed down.
They had been standing on the hawk's head all along.
"Then Long Arrow must be . . ." the doctor looked all around.
"In here! This is a cave!
This rock must have fallen and blocked the entrance!"
The doctor started to bang against the rock.
"Hurry! We don't have much time!" shouted Polynesia.
Dr. Dolittle and Charles tried to push the rock.
It wouldn't budge.
Tommy noticed the bottom of the rock was resting on soft ground.
"Doctor!" he shouted.
"If we remove this dirt, maybe the rock will fall down by itself."
"Good idea, Tommy!" the doctor replied.
They all got on their knees and started to dig away the dirt.
Soon the big rock started to shake back and forth.
"Get out of the way!" cried the doctor.
They watched as the giant rock fell away from the mountain and crashed.
It had indeed been covering the entrance to a cave.
Dr. Dolittle, Polynesia, Tommy, and Charles all peered into the dark cave entrance.
"Hello?" called out the doctor.
"Hello?" came back the echo.
"Maybe we should go inside," the doctor said.
But before they took a step, a tall dark shadow appeared.
It was the great Indian Long Arrow.
He was the tallest man Tommy had ever seen.
He wore a brightly woven cloth round his lower body.
He carried a large pouch around his waist.
Something heavy inside was pulling the pouch downward.
In his hair was a beautiful eagle's feather.
The Indian's eyes were sharp and full of wisdom, just like an eagle's.
He blinked them a few times and stared at Dr. Dolittle.
Dr. Dolittle was speechless.
"Well, I, so . . . ," he stuttered.
The tall Indian did not say a word.
Finally, Dr. Dolittle took a deep breath and said,
"It's a great pleasure to meet you, Long Arrow."
Long Arrow did not open his mouth.
"Oh, how silly of me," gushed the doctor.
"You don't understand me.
Let's see . . . ," the doctor thought for a moment.
Then he started to speak in dog language:
"I am Dr. Dolittle."
The Indian did not understand dog talk.
"I can also speak other animal languages,"
Dr. Dolittle said in horse talk.
The Indian blinked twice but remained silent.
"Dr. Dolittle," interrupted Tommy.
The doctor shook his head.
"Not now, Tommy."
Then he tried pig talk:
"I have heard many great things about you," he said to the Indian.
The Indian scratched his ear.
"Um, Doctor?" Tommy whispered again.
"What is it, Tommy?"
The doctor turned to him impatiently.
"Maybe he understands the eagles' language?" Tommy said shyly.
The doctor nodded.
In eagle talk he said,
"Can you understand me now?"
The Indian's eyes suddenly became warm and friendly.
"At last, we can understand each other,"
Long Arrow said in the eagle language.
Dr. Dolittle and Long Arrow exchanged a long, deep conversation using eagle talk.
Charles covered his ears.
"It sounds like screaming," he said to Tommy.
Tommy agreed.
But Polynesia told them that eagle talk was one of the most beautiful bird languages.
"We have brought you some food and water," the doctor said.
"Thank you," replied Long Arrow as he took the things from the doctor.
But rather than eat and drink, he walked back into the cave.
Dr. Dolittle and Tommy followed him inside.
Polynesia and Charles stayed back at the cave entrance.
It took a while for Tommy's eyes to get used to the dark.
Long Arrow led them to two men lying on the ground.
A little bit of light came through a crack in the ceiling.
Tommy could see that the men were very sick.
Long Arrow said something to them in his native tongue.
Then he opened his pouch and took something out.
It looked like plants and a heavy stone.
He poured water on the plants.
Then he scraped them against the stone to make a paste.
He put the paste on the men's foreheads.
The two men slowly sat up and said something to Long Arrow.
Tommy watched in amazement.
The Indian spoke, and Dr. Dolittle translated.
"He says the men's pain is gone now."
"It's time to go home,"
continued Long Arrow, still speaking in eagle talk.
Long Arrow and Dr. Dolittle helped the two men walk toward the cave entrance.
Tommy carried their things.
"Come to our village," said one man in a weak voice.
"We are grateful to you for saving us," said the other.
But when they reached the entrance, trouble was waiting for them.
A group of the unfriendly natives had tied up Charles and Polynesia.
They pointed their swords at the cave's entrance.
When they saw Dr. Dolittle, they walked toward him angrily.
"Oh no," whispered the doctor.
"What are we going to do?"
Things looked really bad for Dr. Dolittle and his friends.
But then, without warning, someone let out a loud cry.
One native ran toward one of the sick men.
He spoke rapidly.
He had tears in his eyes.
Long Arrow translated for Dr. Dolittle.
"This is the chief's eldest son,"
he said, pointing to one of the sick men.
"His family thought he was dead.
And the other one, the man with the sword, is his younger brother.
Their father, the chief of Popsipetal, has just died."
"What did he die from?" asked the doctor.
"They do not know," translated Long Arrow.
"He was bitten by a mosquito and died soon after."
Dr. Dolittle jumped to his feet.
"A mosquito? Then we must hurry!"
"Ah," Long Arrow said.
"The mosquito must be carrying a disease that spreads through the blood."
Dr. Dolittle nodded.
"Can you help them?" asked Long Arrow.
Dr. Dolittle looked inside his medicine bag.
"How many natives are there?" he asked.
"Over one hundred families," answered Long Arrow.
The doctor sadly shook his head.
"I have some medicine, but not enough for everyone," he said.
"Do not worry," Long Arrow replied.
"I know how to stop the sickness.
But we must hurry before others get sick!"
When they reached the village of Popsipetal, several people ran out toward them crying.
One woman sobbed and spoke to the chief's younger son.
"Her baby is very sick from the same mosquito bite," Long Arrow translated.
Dr. Dolittle looked very upset.
Many others were sick, too.
"Tommy, Charles! I need your help," Dr. Dolittle said.
The natives helped Dr. Dolittle set up a small hut.
All the sick people were put inside the hut.
No one except Dr. Dolittle was allowed inside.
The doctor rolled up his sleeves and began taking care of the people.
Meanwhile Long Arrow had disappeared.
Tommy and Charles brought fresh water and clean cloths to the doctor.
They worked hard all night.
But more and more people got sick.
And Long Arrow still had not returned.
Tommy wondered where the Indian was.
Finally at dawn, the doctor came out of the hut, extremely tired.
"That's it," he sighed.
"There is no more medicine left."
"But what about all these people?"
Tommy looked at the long line standing in front of the hut.
They were waiting to be treated.
"There must be something you can do," cried Charles.
"I don't know," the doctor said sadly.
"I can't help them anymore."
With those words, the doctor began to cry.
Suddenly the sky began to rumble.
Everyone looked up to see what was causing the sounds.
A large band of eagles flew across the village and into the woods.
They screeched loudly as they soared high up and dived down low.
"What are they saying?" Tommy asked the doctor.
"It is a miracle." Dr. Dolittle smiled.
"The eagles are eating up all the mosquitoes!"
"They taste rather disgusting," screamed one eagle.
"Not much flavor," complained another.
"They're not as bad as flies," said a third.
Dr. Dolittle clapped his hands excitedly and yelled,
"Thank you! Thank you for saving the people!"
"That little human is speaking our language," said the first eagle.
"Yes, that's the famous Dr. Dolittle," the second one said.
"Oh, the one Long Arrow told us about," said the third.
"It was Long Arrow who has saved you, not us!" they shouted.
Just then the largest, grandest eagle flew over them.
Sitting on its back was Long Arrow.
"I have returned,"
Long Arrow said to the doctor, getting off the eagle.
"Now give this to every person and they will be sick no more."
He held out a large jar of herbs and plants.
For the next two days, Dr. Dolittle and Long Arrow worked together curing the natives.
Soon not one person in the village of Popsipetal was sick.
Dr. Dolittle and his friends stayed on Spider Monkey Island for over a month.
During that time, Dr. Dolittle and Long Arrow spent many days learning from each other.
Long Arrow taught the doctor about herbs and plants.
"Do not touch the leaves on this one," the Indian said in eagle talk.
"Only pick it by its stem."
Dr. Dolittle taught Long Arrow about modern medicine.
"Put this in your ears," he said.
The doctor held up a stethoscope and passed it to the Indian.
He held the metal disc against Long Arrow's chest.
Long Arrow jumped back in fear.
"Don't worry," laughed Dr. Dolittle.
"That's the sound of your heart beating."
As the days went by, Tommy noticed it getting colder and colder.
"Brrrr," he shivered.
"It feels like winter."
"Yes, I noticed that, too," the doctor remarked.
He looked around the village of Popsipetal.
People everywhere seemed to be trembling and shaking from the cold.
Dr. Dolittle and Tommy walked to the beach.
They saw a large flock of birds shivering in the cold.
"Dr. Dolittle!" called out Polynesia.
Tommy noticed that her beak was blue and her wings were shaking.
"What's going on here, Polynesia?" the doctor looked around.
"They're all leaving,"
she replied, pointing to the birds.
"It's too cold for them to live here."
"But what is causing this sudden cold?" the doctor asked aloud.
"It's the island, Doctor," answered the parrot.
"Spider Monkey Island is a floating island."
Dr. Dolittle slapped his knee.
"That's right! So we must be moving south."
"Are we moving toward the South Pole?" asked Polynesia.
"It seems that way," the doctor answered.
"We must turn around, Doctor," said Tommy urgently.
"The Popsipetal people and the animals can't survive in a cold climate."
As soon as Tommy had spoken, all the animals started to come out of the forest.
There were monkeys, opossums, butterflies, pigs, and all kinds of insects.
"Please help us, Dr. Dolittle," said one monkey.
"We're all so cold."
"All the plants and fruits are freezing," cried an opossum.
"There is nothing to eat."
Dr. Dolittle thought and thought about what he could do.
"Polynesia," he said finally, "we need the help of some whales."
"Whales?" asked Tommy.
"Whales are big strong creatures," explained the doctor.
"Perhaps they can push the island back north."
So Polynesia and some other birds flew off in search of whales.
Shortly, Polynesia returned with two dolphins.
"I asked for whales, Polynesia," sighed the doctor.
"Not to worry, Dr. Dolittle," said one dolphin.
"The whales are already in the back pushing you along."
"But I can't feel anything," said Tommy.
The dolphins stared at him with open mouths.
"He can speak our language, too?" they cried.
"Yes, he's very clever," the doctor said proudly.
"Now, how many whales are there?"
"We were lucky, and ran into a large herd," replied Polynesia.
"Good work, Polynesia," smiled the doctor.
"We should soon be heading back north."
All the animals, birds, and other creatures cheered loudly.
Tommy wanted to ask the dolphins,
"Why does this island float?"
But he made a mistake in dolphin language and said instead,
"Do your toes float in water?"
Dr. Dolittle, Polynesia, and the dolphins could not stop laughing.
Poor Tommy turned bright red.
He asked again, correctly this time.
A big dolphin explained:
"Spider Monkey Island used to be a part of a large piece of land.
But for some reason it broke away and fell into the water.
Only part of the island is above the water.
The other, bigger half is underwater."
Another dolphin continued: "See all those mountains.
For some strange reason, they are hollow.
When the land fell into the water, the air inside stopped it from sinking.
That is why the island floats."
"Just like a balloon," Tommy exclaimed.
"There must be a way to stop the island from floating," said Dr. Dolittle.
"We need to get the air out of the mountains," said Polynesia.
"But how?" asked Tommy.
Everyone thought, but no one could come up with a solution.
Dr. Dolittle told Long Arrow what the dolphins had said.
The Indian listened quietly then replied with two words: "Follow me."
So Dr. Dolittle and his friends did as he asked.
Long Arrow had lived on Spider Monkey Island for over three years.
He had discovered many places that even the natives did not know about.
He knew one that was especially interesting.
But they had to walk all day to get to it.
Tommy's feet hurt, but he did not complain.
Finally, Long Arrow stopped in the darkest part of the forest.
Tommy could barely see his hands in front of him.
"Over there." Long Arrow pointed upward.
Everyone looked up.
Beyond the tree tops they saw a very high mountain, the highest on the island.
On the edge of its cliff sat an enormous rock.
"It looks like it's going to fall," cried Charles.
Everyone agreed with him.
"I call that the hanging stone," said Long Arrow.
"It will help the island stop floating."
"How?" asked Charles.
But Long Arrow was already walking ahead.
They walked for many more hours.
Now Tommy was hungry, but he wasn't shivering.
"Dr. Dolittle," he said,
"I don't feel so cold anymore."
"Yes, I noticed that, too," the doctor replied.
"We must be moving toward warmer climates."
Long Arrow led them into an open area.
The surface was rocky and hard.
As they moved toward the center, they noticed a huge hole in the ground.
Dr. Dolittle bent down and looked into the hole.
"Amazing!" he said, and his voice echoed deep and long.
Charles bravely looked down the hole.
It was so deep that you could not see the bottom.
Dr. Dolittle stood next to him and said: "This must be an opening into the hollow area under the mountains."
"And look!" Charles pointed up excitedly.
The hanging stone was right above the huge hole.
Dr. Dolittle looked at Long Arrow.
"I understand now," the doctor said.
Tommy and Charles looked puzzled.
"If the hanging stone falls into this hole," the doctor explained, "it will drop all the way through the island.
When it hits the bottom, it will crack the hollow and the ocean will flood in."
Charles shook his head.
"What if it sinks the whole island?" he asked.
The doctor thought about Charles' words.
"We will need to find a place where the ocean is not so deep," he replied.
"Then the island will sink a little.
But there will still be lots of land sticking up above the waves."
Tommy clearly understood now.
"Come, Tommy," said the doctor, "we must tell the whales.
The whales can help us find a place."
Dr. Dolittle and Tommy ran to the other side of the mountain.
From where they stood, Tommy could see waves and water splashing everywhere.
It was the herd of whales working hard.
"Hello?" the doctor called out.
A large gray head popped up and sprayed water out through its blowhole.
The size and strength of the great creature made Tommy tremble.
Dr. Dolittle, however, was not afraid.
He walked up and said a few words to the whale.
The whale let out a loud sound through its blowhole.
Soon a series of toots were heard from all the other whales.
Dr. Dolittle turned back toward Tommy.
"Now we must return to the village," he said.
A few days later, Dr. Dolittle gathered all the Popsipetal people near the hanging stone.
Through Long Arrow, he explained what they were going to do.
In his hand Dr. Dolittle held a large stick.
He lifted it high and then, giving the signal, he dropped his hand.
Everyone started to stamp their feet and play the drums as loudly as they could.
The ground began to rumble and shake.
But the stone did not move.
"Louder!" shouted the doctor.
Tommy felt his feet moving on the shaking ground.
Suddenly from the sky came a sound like thunder.
Long Arrow was riding on an eagle and leading hundreds of the birds toward the stone.
The eagles called out with loud screeches.
They flew past the stone so fast that they created a strong wind.
The hanging stone began to sway back and forth.
A few moments later, the huge stone fell off the cliff and into the hole.
Everyone stopped and waited holding their breath.
Then the entire island shook as if a volcano had erupted.
Spider Monkey Island was covered in clouds of dust and dirt.
There was a loud hissing noise and eagle feathers everywhere.
Everyone's feet and hands hurt from drumming and stamping their feet.
Dr. Dolittle and Long Arrow looked over the cliff.
The hanging stone had fallen exactly into the hole.
"We did it, my friend!"
shouted the doctor in a hoarse voice.
"That hissing noise is the air rushing out of the hole.
The hollow is filling with water."
They stood up and shook each other's hands.
The island was no longer floating.
One by one the people of Popsipetal came before the doctor.
Each of them bowed and then placed their right hand on his shoulder.
Dr. Dolittle did not understand what they were doing.
Finally the chief's eldest son, the one Dr. Dolittle and Long Arrow had saved, came up to him.
He wore a long robe with a red sash across his right shoulder.
He carried a large wreath made of eagle feathers.
He removed the sash and placed it on Dr. Dolittle's shoulder.
"What is the meaning of this?" the doctor cried.
Long Arrow translated for the chief's son.
"A chief may care deeply about his people.
A chief may be brave enough to do foolish things.
A chief may have great talents, like speaking to animals.
But a king is a man who has all of these things.
Hail King Jong!"
"But who is this King Jong?" asked the doctor.
"You are," answered Long Arrow.
With that, the chief's son placed the crown of eagle feathers on the doctor's head.
All the people began bowing and chanting "Zanming Jong! Zanming Jong!"
This meant, "Long live King Jong."
So on that day, Dr. Dolittle became the king of Popsipetal.
But he was not a very happy king.
King Jong was not allowed to go anywhere by himself.
There were many duties for the king to carry out.
Every day, the villagers came to the king with their problems.
Long Arrow translated for them.
"This man wants permission to plant more vegetables," he explained.
"Oh, who cares," murmured the king.
"Let him do whatever he wants."
Every day, King Jong had lessons in the Popsipetal language.
Learning animal languages was quite easy and fun.
But King Jong found human languages difficult and boring.
"Lu, la, lick, lur," he repeated.
The king was always busy.
So Tommy missed Dr. Dolittle very much.
"Are you sleeping, Tommy?"
Polynesia whispered in the dark.
"No," he answered.
"Tommy, we must get the doctor out of here," she said.
"He's so miserable."
"But what can we do?
He always has those bodyguards around," Tommy said.
"Tomorrow when Dr. Dolittle hears the people's problems, you will approach him," said Polynesia.
"What should I say?" asked Tommy.
"This is what you will say."
She whispered something into Tommy's ear.
The next day, King Jong sat on his throne again.
How surprised and happy he was to see Tommy approach him.
"Tommy!" he cried joyfully.
Tommy bowed low and spoke in the dolphins' language.
King Jong listened carefully and said, "I will be waiting."
That evening, King Jong went to bed at the usual time.
His bodyguards stood in front of the hut.
They did not notice two spiders weaving a web above their heads.
They also did not see the two small mice hiding in the trees with Polynesia.
When she gave the signal, each mouse bit hard on the guards' toes.
But before the guards could scream, the spiders swung their webs over their mouths and eyes.
Polynesia flew inside the hut.
Dr. Dolittle was dressed in his regular clothes.
"We must hurry, Doctor," she whispered.
"What about Tommy? Charles? Long Arrow?" he asked.
"They'll meet us," Polynesia assured him.
Together they ran out of the hut and disappeared into the woods.
Dr. Dolittle and Polynesia arrived on the beach.
Tommy was so happy to see the doctor that he began to cry.
"Hush, now," the doctor said, comforting him.
"It's good to have you back, Dr. Dolittle,"
Charles said as he brushed away a tear.
"We must get going before the natives find you are missing," said Polynesia.
"Will the people be all right?"
the doctor asked, looking back toward the huts.
"Of course," answered Long Arrow.
"They already have a chief.
Do not worry, I will explain to them."
"You're not coming with us?" the doctor said in surprise.
"I'm afraid not, my friend," the Indian said sadly.
"My journey is different from yours.
You must go your way, and I must go mine."
The two men did not speak for a minute.
"Will we ever meet again?" asked Dr. Dolittle.
"As long as the eagles soar, our paths shall cross," replied Long Arrow.
A loud splash came from the waters.
"He is here," Polynesia said.
"Who is?" asked the doctor.
"Remember what the fidgit said?"
Tommy grabbed the doctor's hand excitedly.
"He spoke about the great glass sea snail?"
Tommy led the doctor toward the edge of the water.
Dr. Dolittle stopped in his tracks and gasped at the creature before him.
It was an enormous snail, the size of two large houses.
Its shell was transparent and shone like a million diamonds.
"It's beautiful!" sighed the doctor.
"How did you find it?"
"When we told Long Arrow you wanted to learn shellfish language," explained Tommy, "Long Arrow went in search of the snail."
Dr. Dolittle smiled at Long Arrow.
"Now you can learn the language on your way back home," said Tommy.
"What? Will the snail come with us?" the doctor said, confused.
The snail let out a loud groan and shook its huge body.
The bottom of its shell came away from its body.
Dr. Dolittle's eyes grew big with excitement.
"You and your friends can ride inside the shell," Long Arrow explained.
"The snail will take you on an underwater journey."
Dr. Dolittle wiped a tear from his eye.
"How can I ever thank you?" he said with emotion.
"You are my dearest friend."
Dr. Dolittle blew his nose.
"You have made all my dreams come true."
Tommy felt a lump in his throat.
He looked around the island.
The sun was starting to come up.
He realized that he had learned much more on this voyage than he had ever expected.
But he also realized how much he missed his parents and Puddleby.
He was ready to go home.
It was very sad to say good-bye to Long Arrow.
He had a gift for each of his new friends.
To Charles he gave a beautiful stone with a red dot in the middle.
To Tommy he gave a large eagle's feather.
Tommy wore it in his hair, just like Long Arrow.
For Polynesia, Long Arrow had a tiny necklace made of flowers.
She wore it proudly around her neck.
And finally, to Dr. Dolittle Long Arrow gave his pouch.
"I can't accept this," the doctor said, his voice choking.
"It is my most treasured item," said the Indian,
"and I want my most treasured friend to have it."
The two friends cried as they finally said good-bye.
Dr. Dolittle and his friends climbed into the sea snail's shell.
Inside the shell, it was comfortably warm.
There were no chairs, but Tommy found that the snail's back was soft to sit on.
He looked outside.
It felt strange to view the world from inside a shell.
After everyone was settled in, the snail groaned once again.
Its shell locked in place and slowly it moved into the water.
Dr. Dolittle and his friends waved to Long Arrow as they disappeared below the waves.
"Now the real voyage begins!" Charles shouted joyfully.
Yes, returning home was yet another adventure.
After returning to Puddleby, Tommy's life changed quite a bit.
He could now speak more animal languages.
He was no longer afraid of any kind of animal.
And he was certain that he wanted to be an animal doctor when he grew up.
But some things would never change.
"Tommy! Come listen to this!"
the doctor would shout excitedly, pulling his head out of the shellfish tank.
"I think I've got it!"
Whenever Charles came to visit, Dr. Dolittle and his friends would talk about their trip.
The other pets never got tired of hearing all the exciting stories.
But Tommy was ready for a new voyage.
During one of Charles' visits, Dr. Dolittle looked at Tommy and winked.
It seemed as if Dr. Dolittle were ready too.
Tommy thought of places they could travel.
It didn't matter where they went.
As long as Tommy was with Dr. Dolittle, every voyage would be an adventure.
